papers.title: Slow-Wave Enhancement Reduces Axonal Injury in Murine Traumatic Brain Injury.
papers.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a major cause of death and disability as well as impaired cognition and sleep-wake abnormalities. The pathological hallmark of TBI is disturbed axonal transport and accumulation of proteins, leading to diffuse axonal injury (DAI). Recent studies suggest a role for slow-wave sleep (SWS) in the clearance of harmful extracellular proteins and functional recovery. Our group previously found that increasing SWS after TBI in rats improved cognition and decreased accumulation of injury-related histological markers in cortex and hippocampus, indicating a neuroprotective role of SWS. Though growing evidence suggests that sleep can improve the outcome of TBI, prior mouse models of TBI were incompatible with sleep recordings. In the current study, we modified the classical weight-drop mouse model to be compatible with a headset for recording electroencephalogram (EEG) and electromyogram, and to replicate effects of SWS modulation on TBI outcome measures. The resulting mild TBI mouse model shows cognitive impairment, EEG abnormalities, and DAI. Such DAI was reduced following treatment with sodium oxybate during the first 3 days after trauma, concomitant with increased slow-wave activity. Chemogenetic modulation of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons, on the other hand, did not reduce slow-wave activity. Overall, in the present study, we characterized an adapted weight-drop mouse TBI model for studying the relationship between sleep and TBI and provided additional evidence on involvement of sleep in neuronal recovery.

papers.title: Comparison and extension of the Riemannian Procrustes analysis and tangent space alignment transfer learning methods.
papers.abstract: This study compares Riemannian Procrustes analysis (RPA) and tangent space alignment (TSA) for transfer learning of motor-imagery EEG data. The study also examines how performance changes when the EEG data is represented using analytic Hermitian positive definite covariance matrices instead of standard symmetric positive definite covariance matrices.Approach. The methods' geometric constraints were compared and explained. Additionally, the methods were evaluated in two scenarios on real EEG data, one with substantial target-domain knowledge and one calibration-like with a limited amount of training data and thus limited target-domain knowledge. Six public EEG datasets with multiple subjects performing two or multiple motor imagery tasks were used. We report paired comparisons of classification performance for the different transfer learning methods and covariance matrix representations across the datasets in order to draw general conclusions about performance.Main results. In the scenario with substantial target-domain knowledge, the TSA method outperformed the RPA method, and representing the EEG data as analytical covariance matrices outperformed standard covariance matrices. In the scenario with limited target-domain knowledge, performance depended on the amount of available target data, and source-data selection emerged as an important component of successful transfer learning. Significance. This study gives a deeper understanding of TSA and RPA transfer learning methods commonly used in brain-computer interfaces, which may inform future research and implementation. The analysis also demonstrates the importance of source data selection in brain-computer interface transfer learning.

papers.title: EEG-Derived Proxies of Cortical Excitability in Epilepsy: Group Discrimination, Temporal Stability and Medication Sensitivity
papers.abstract: Objective To identify EEG-derived markers of cortical excitability that best distinguish people with epilepsy from healthy controls while maintaining stability across repeated recordings, and to assess the influence of antiseizure medication (ASM) burden on these measures. Methods Scalp EEG recordings from the Temple University Hospital EEG Epilepsy Corpus were analyzed, including 1,404 recordings from 96 individuals with neurologist-confirmed epilepsy and 85 healthy controls across multiple sessions. Eight global EEG measures were evaluated: aperiodic exponent and offset, sample entropy, detrended fluctuation analysis exponent and derived index, spatial gamma-band phase consistency, and absolute and relative alpha power. Primary group inference used linear mixed-effects models to account for repeated recordings and sessions within participants. Secondary analyses examined group differences in measures temporal stability and cross-metric correlation. We examined only in epilepsy group associations between EEG-derived metrics and ASMs count, and their impact on cross-metric correlations. Results In the mixed-effects models, aperiodic offset and exponent were the only measures with FDR-robust group effects. Aperiodic offset showed higher consistency in epilepsy than in healthy controls (standardized epilepsy-minus-healthy beta = 0.52, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.78, FDR-adjusted p = 0.001). Across sessions, consistency was higher in epilepsy for aperiodic offset exponent (beta = 0.32, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.54, FDR-adjusted p = 0.018). Cross-metric correlation patterns were largely preserved between groups. Medication associations were examined separately within the epilepsy group. Higher ASM burden was associated with higher alpha relative power. Significance Among eight candidate EEG measures aperiodic offset and exponent differed between groups (epilepsy vs. healthy controls), and both were more reproducible across sessions in epilepsy. Relative alpha power tracked within-person antiseizure medication burden, suggesting that disease-related and treatment-related EEG markers may be complementary. These findings, obtained from routine clinical EEG in an open dataset, suggest aperiodic spectral parameters as candidates for prospective validation as biomarkers.

papers.title: iEEG Can Help EEG: Improving Clinical Scalp EEG Analysis through Intracranial Priors
papers.abstract: Scalp electroencephalography (EEG) is a cornerstone of clinical brain monitoring, making the quality of its signal fundamental to downstream tasks and models. However, that signal is heavily contaminated by non-neural interference and blurred by volume conduction. Existing methods operate almost exclusively within the scalp modality, so they inherit the contamination they would need to overcome. In practice, intracranial EEG (iEEG) observes the neural activity with far higher fidelity, yet it is invasive and therefore scarce, and the two modalities are rarely recorded as pairs at scale, share no common channel space, and offer no clean ground truth to directly supervise a mapping. Motivated by the neuronal synchronization mechanism shared by the two modalities, we propose a reprogramming approach that fits a signal-to-signal model on iEEG alone and freezes it as a cross-modal prior. We introduce ReBrain, a framework to transfer an iEEG-learned prior to scalp EEG, which re-expresses any scalp signal through that prior and can be inserted upstream of any downstream model with no pairing or fine-tuning. ReBrain consistently improves host models across recordings from multiple hospitals and across architecture families, and our analysis traces this gain to genuine neural structure carried by iEEG rather than to the architecture itself. This work provides evidence that a scarce clean modality can serve as a transferable prior for an abundant noisy one, offering a general recipe for cross-modal transfer among biosignals. Our code is available at https://github.com/Xianglong-Bao/ReBrain.

papers.title: Frequency-Specific Thalamocortical Network Dynamics During Focal Seizures in Humans.
papers.abstract: The thalamus is an emerging neuromodulation target in drug-resistant focal epilepsy because of its frequent ictal involvement. However, frequency-specific and directional thalamocortical dynamics remain poorly understood. We sought to characterize thalamocortical network dynamics across seizure evolution using stereoelectroencephalography (SEEG). We retrospectively analyzed SEEG recordings from patients with pediatric-onset drug-resistant focal epilepsy with simultaneous cortical and thalamic sampling focusing on the anterior nucleus (AN) and centromedian nucleus (CM). We applied visual analysis with quantitative measures of spectral power, imaginary coherence, and spectral Granger causality across slow (1-12 Hz), β (13-30 Hz), and γ (30-70 Hz) bands to quantify thalamocortical and cortico-cortical interactions from seizure onset to termination. Random forest models were trained to classify seizure state using thalamic EEG features as an exploratory analysis. The final cohort comprised 19 patients (median age, 16.9 years; 31.6% female), with 66 focal seizures analyzed. Thalamic ictal activity was present at seizure onset in 81% of sampled thalamic contacts and became nearly universal by seizure termination. Both the thalamus and seizure onset zone showed increased spectral power during seizures, with prominent slow-band augmentation at seizure termination in the thalamus. Similarly, thalamocortical imaginary coherence increased during seizures, with the largest changes near seizure termination in the slow band (AN-SOZ: 11% [IQR, 2 to 20], rank-biserial correlations (rrb) = 0.84; CM-SOZ: 12% [IQR, 3 to 23], rrb = 0.84) and β band (AN-SOZ: 5% [IQR, 0 to 12], rrb = 0.74; CM-SOZ: 8% [IQR, 2 to 15], rrb = 0.86). Directed connectivity analyses demonstrated bidirectional thalamocortical interactions, with large slow-frequency thalamus-to-SOZ outflow near seizure termination from both AN and CM, exceeding propagation-zone-to-SOZ cortico-cortical flow (both p < 0.01). Seizure state was classified using thalamic EEG features, with area under the receiver operating characteristic curve values of 0.825 for AN and 0.839 for CM. Human focal seizures engage frequency-specific and bidirectional thalamocortical interactions that evolve from onset to termination. These findings support the thalamus as a source of clinically relevant seizure-state information and may inform thalamic biomarker development for neuromodulation in drug-resistant epilepsy.

papers.title: Best1 shapes the depth and stability of NREM sleep.
papers.abstract: Sleep architecture is orchestrated by neuronal circuits, yet the contribution of astrocytes-particularly to the depth and continuity of sleep-remains incompletely understood. Mammalian sleep is composed of rapid eye movement (REM) and non-REM (NREM) stages, with NREM further subdivided into light and deep phases. While neuronal and neurotransmitter-based mechanisms of sleep regulation have been extensively characterized, the role of astrocytic signaling in deep NREM sleep has received relatively little attention. Bestrophin-1 (Best1) is a calcium-activated anion channel highly enriched in astrocytes, known to mediate non-vesicular release of gliotransmitters such as glutamate, D-serine, and GABA, and to influence neuronal excitability. Here, we identify Best1 as a critical regulator of deep NREM sleep. Immunohistochemistry revealed robust Best1 expression in astrocytes across sleep-regulating brain regions. EEG/EMG polysomnography in Best1 knockout (Best1-KO) mice demonstrated a selective disruption of deep NREM sleep, despite preserved total sleep time and overall NREM duration. Best1-KO mice exhibited shorter deep NREM bouts, attenuated delta-band (0.5-4 Hz) EEG power, and altered vigilance-state transitions, with reduced entry into and maintenance of deep NREM. Sleep trajectories were biased toward Wake → light NREM → REM transitions, frequently bypassing deep sleep stages. Spectral decomposition further confirmed diminished delta oscillations during NREM episodes. These findings establish Best1 as a substage-specific molecular gatekeeper of deep NREM sleep. By uncovering a glial mechanism that shapes sleep sub-architecture, this work highlights astrocytic ion signaling as a promising therapeutic target for disorders marked by fragmented or insufficient deep sleep, including those associated with aging and neurodegenerative disease.

papers.title: Comparison of Infradian and Circadian Rhythms in Laboratory Rodents.
papers.abstract: Infradian cycles are multi-day oscillations whose mechanisms are still poorly understood, while circadian rhythms have been extensively studied and are well-documented in mammals. In this study, we monitored the locomotor activity of three rodent species: CD-1 mice (Mus musculus), Mongolian gerbils (Meriones unguiculatus), and white-tailed antelope squirrels (Ammospermophilus leucurus). We used Lomb-Scargle spectral analysis to verify the prevalence of circadian and infradian rhythms, the magnitude of the spectral power, and associations across species, rhythms, and sexes. Circadian rhythms were robust and were found for all animals. For infradian rhythms, the prevalence in mice was extremely low, whereas the prevalence in gerbils and squirrels was moderate in the 5- and 10-day ranges. In all cases, the strength of infradian rhythmicity was less than 10% of the strength of circadian rhythmicity. As no natural environmental cycle is documented to operate in the 5- to 10-day range, further studies are needed to determine whether an endogenous source may account for this weak but significant infradian rhythmicity.

papers.title: Evidence for decoder-label-regime-dependent effects of complementary leaky integrate-and-fire temporal-state decoding in motor-imagery EEG.
papers.abstract: Motor-imagery electroencephalography often provides limited subject-specific supervision. This study tested whether complementary leaky integrate-and-fire (CLIF)-family temporal-state decoding shows a decoder-level advantage after the EEG representation is fixed, how that advantage changes with decoder-label availability, and whether hard binary spikes are required. ANN-SEW, the artificial neural network comparator with spike-element-wise (SEW) residual topology, and SEW-CLIF received identical frozen attention-based temporal convolutional network (ATCNet) and filter-bank convolutional network (FBCNet) representations. The evidence chain combined BCI Competition IV Dataset 2a (BCI2a) development, retrospective OpenBMI replication, an internally pre-access-held-out BCI Competition IV Dataset 2b (BCI2b) evaluation, cross-entropy-only label-budget analyses, and a separate internally pre-access-locked BNCI2015-001 Session-A-to-Session-B evaluation. Additional robustness analyses included shared whole-sequence readout for parameter-matched gated recurrent unit (GRU) and temporal convolutional network (TCN) decoders, exact-gradient sigmoid-gated Soft-CLIF, equal optimizer-update budgets, a within-BCI2a binary sensitivity analysis, and computational profiling. Under cross-entropy-only training, SEW-CLIF exceeded ANN-SEW by 10.082 percentage points (pp) on BCI2a and 5.470 pp. on OpenBMI, while full-budget BCI2b remained near parity (+0.181 pp). The ANN-relative gap decreased as decoder labels increased and persisted under equal-update training. At 25 labels/class, exact-gradient Soft-CLIF exceeded ANN-SEW by 11.085, 8.479, and 5.809 pp. on BCI2a, BCI2b, and OpenBMI, respectively. With matched whole-sequence readout, hard SEW-CLIF was broadly comparable to GRU-Stat and TCN-Stat on BCI2a and BCI2b and modestly higher on OpenBMI. The internally pre-access-locked BNCI2015-001 evaluation showed the same attenuation, with a slope of -2.319 pp. per label doubling (95% CI, -4.118 to -0.604). CLIF-family temporal-state dynamics show a reproducible decoder-label-regime effect under frozen supervised representations. Hard forward discretization is not required for the ANN-relative effect, and matched temporal readout substantially reduces differences between CLIF and other continuous temporal decoders.

papers.title: Image-grounded encoding models reveal distinct temporal profiles of naturalistic object and scene processing in the human brain
papers.abstract: In real-world vision, the human brain needs to process large amounts of information to effectively interact with its environment. It is well established that our visual system has specialized regions to process information efficiently, such as scene-, face-, and object-selective areas, which can be uncovered using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). However, functional localizers typically use artificially separated stimuli (e.g. scene backgrounds vs. object cutouts), and fMRI signals are insensitive to potential temporal processing differences. Here, we identify temporal signatures of object and scene processing in real-world visual environments by building image-grounded brain-predictive encoding models of human electroencephalography (EEG) responses. In a large set of high-resolution natural images, we first separate object-bound from scene-bound features on a per-image basis, and then used these features to train separate deep neural network-based encoding models to predict EEG responses to the full, intact images. We find that encoding models trained on object-bound features consistently exhibit a delayed temporal encoding profile compared to models trained on scene-bound features. Control analyses confirm the robustness of this delayed object encoding, showing that a consistent separation of objects from scene parts is needed to achieve a temporal distinction. Using these distinct encoding profiles as processing templates, we reveal the typicality of individual image elements as objects or part of the scene. These findings demonstrate that object and scene processing in the human brain unfold differentially over time and indicate that image-grounded encoding models are helpful tools for isolating components of naturalistic visual perception.

papers.title: Investigating Modified Deep Learning Models for Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder Classification Using Electroencephalography Spectrograms.
papers.abstract: This study developed neurophysiologically informed data augmentation strategies to improve electroencephalogram (EEG)-based deep learning classification of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in children with limited labeled EEG data. ADHD affects approximately 8.0% of children and adolescents worldwide, or about 129 million individuals aged 5-19 years. Clinical diagnosis relies largely on behavioral observations; EEG provides objective biomarkers, but conventional image augmentation may not preserve disease-relevant neural oscillation patterns. We introduced band-shuffle augmentation, which exchanges selected spectral content between samples within the same diagnostic class at the level of canonical EEG frequency bands. The method was evaluated through systematic architecture optimization, augmentation experiments, and integration into an adaptive multistrategy training pipeline. Band-shuffle augmentation achieved 75.05% validation accuracy, 75.76% F1 score, 75.30% sensitivity, and 74.56% specificity, exceeding the 74.32% accuracy of traditional computer vision augmentation. The integrated multistrategy framework achieved 77.47% validation accuracy and 0.8414 AUC, improving accuracy by 27.0% over the 60.99% MobileNetV2 baseline and by 4.2% over conventional augmentation. The results support frequency band-level augmentation as a neurophysiologically informed approach to EEG spectrogram classification. Ablation indicated distinct module contributions, and Grad-CAM highlighted frequency-specific regions consistent with ADHD neurophysiology. This framework may support EEG-based computer-aided screening, although external validation is required before clinical use.

papers.title: Motor Imagery Classification Using Hybrid Cross-Subject Class Mixup and Selective Attention
papers.abstract: Motor imagery (MI) enables a brain-computer interface (BCI) to decode movement intentions without overt movement. Hybrid electroencephalography (EEG) and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) classification combines complementary signals, but inter-subject variability and the design of information exchange between modalities affect generalization to new subjects. We propose a framework that combines Cross-Subject Class Mixup (CSCM) with Selective Attention. CSCM aims to construct new training data to make the model robust against inter-subject variability. It independently selects EEG and fNIRS donor trials from other training subjects within the anchor class and mixes each modality while preserving the original label. Selective Attention provides an effective way to simultaneously model the temporal signal characteristics and fuse the two modalities. It retains causal temporal self-attention for EEG and uses a classification token (CLS) to integrate both modalities, without fNIRS attention updates or direct cross-modal temporal-token attention. Leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) evaluation across 28 subjects on a public EEG-fNIRS dataset yields a mean balanced accuracy (BA) of 76.85% and a macro-averaged F1 score (Macro-F1) of 76.58%. The proposed model achieves the highest mean performance among five reimplemented baselines. We also examine the contributions of CSCM and Selective Attention through modality-specific mixing and donor-policy comparisons, temporal-policy comparisons, interventions on direct cross-modal paths, and component ablations.

papers.title: Electroencephalography-derived spectral edge frequency 95 targets in toddlers under propofol anaesthesia✰.
papers.abstract: Proprietary processed EEG indices are less accurate in young children. We evaluated spectral edge frequency 95 (SEF95), a nonproprietary EEG index representing the frequency below which 95% of total EEG power resides, to establish target thresholds for varying anaesthetic depths during propofol anaesthesia in toddlers. Secondary objectives were to assess the relationship between SEF95 and plasma propofol concentration, and to evaluate airway reactivity during laryngoscopy. In this prospective study of toddlers aged 13 to 24 months, Dixon's up-and-down method and centred isotonic regression were used to determine the SEF95 targets for 50% (ED50) and 90% (ED90) probability of nonresponse to three clinical stimuli: pacifier placement (assessing consciousness), electrical nerve stimulation (nociception), and laryngoscopy (intubation readiness). Linear mixed-effects regression was used to analyse the association between plasma propofol concentration and SEF95. Among 51 toddlers, SEF95 ED50 and ED90 targets (Hz) were 21.8 (90% CI 20.8-23.4) and 20.3 (19.1-20.7) Hz for pacifier placement, 12.0 (10.8-18.3) and 10.4 (8.7-11.3) Hz for electrical stimulation, and 10.3 (4.6-11.8) and 4.4 (1.5-5.4) Hz for laryngoscopy. Each 1 Hz increase in SEF95 corresponded to a 0.21 μg ml-1 decrease in plasma propofol (r=0.46, P<0.001), as described by the equation: plasma propofol concentration (μg ml-1)=5.80-0.21×SEF95 (Hz). This study defined EEG SEF95 targets for loss of consciousness, response to noxious stimuli, and intubation readiness in toddlers aged 13 to 24 months. When combined with existing infant data, these age-specific SEF95 targets can optimise propofol titration and dosing accuracy during EEG-guided propofol anaesthesia in patients aged <2 yr. NCT05701748. Registered 17 January 2023; PI: Ian Yuan.

papers.title: Signatures of Performance Monitoring in Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder and At-risk Groups: Midfrontal Theta Predicts Divergent Behavioral Adaptation.
papers.abstract: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) has been robustly linked to increased performance monitoring, most consistently indexed by an increased error-related negativity (ERN). However, the role of response-related midfrontal theta oscillations, a key neural mechanism supporting cognitive control and behavioral adaptation, remains incompletely understood in OCD and at-risk populations. EEG was recorded from 180 adults (46 OCD, 39 unaffected first-degree relatives, 39 with adverse childhood experiences, and 56 controls) during an arrowhead flanker task. Response-related midfrontal theta power (4-7 Hz) was investigated alongside behavioral indices, including error rates and post-error slowing. Group differences in neural and behavioral data, trial-wise theta-behavior relationship, and associations with clinical symptoms were investigated. Error-related increases in midfrontal theta were robust across participants. Relative to the combined non-OCD sample, individuals with OCD exhibited enhanced error-related theta power, while unaffected first-degree relatives and individuals with adverse childhood experiences did not differ from controls. Single-trial analyses revealed altered neural-behavioral coupling: greater theta predicted slower and less accurate performance on subsequent trials in OCD, and, contrarily, improved subsequent performance in controls. Consistent with these findings, individuals with OCD showed prolonged post-error slowing. Across participants, error rate and PES were associated with worry and depressive symptoms, whereas theta power was associated with age and depressive symptoms. OCD is characterized by enhanced error-related midfrontal theta together with an altered association between neural error signals and adaptive behavioral adjustment. These findings suggest that abnormal performance monitoring in OCD reflects not only exaggerated error processing but also disrupted implementation of cognitive control.

papers.title: MyoGen: unified biophysical modeling of human neuromotor activity and resulting signals.
papers.abstract: Understanding human motor control requires integrating cortical and spinal activity, muscle mechanics, and electrophysiology, which are typically studied in isolation. We present MyoGen, an open-source framework that unifies spinal circuitry, proprioceptive feedback, musculotendon dynamics, and multimodal electromyography generation. Using data-driven optimization benchmarked against human motor unit recordings, MyoGen produces motor unit population activity matching experimental discharge-rate distributions and variability across muscles. The framework generates decomposable surface and intramuscular electromyography, reproduces beta-band modulation of descending drive and its transformation into force, and implements key sensorimotor loop components. Dimensionality reduction of simulated agonist-antagonist electromyography reveals low-dimensional control manifolds consistent with recordings from able-bodied individuals and those with spinal cord injury. Here, we show that MyoGen provides a physiologically grounded simulation substrate, enabling systematic investigation of motor control principles, benchmarking of signal-processing algorithms, and exploration of experimentally inaccessible sensorimotor interactions.

papers.title: Knockdown of KCNQ2 in CA1 reshapes epilepsy-related limbic network rhythms and reduces spontaneous exploratory behavior in mice.
papers.abstract: Circuit-level effects of localized cornu ammonis 1 (CA1) potassium voltage-gated channel subfamily Q member 2 (KCNQ2) loss-of-function on epileptogenesis remain poorly understood, despite the well-established association of KCNQ2 deficiency with epilepsy and neuropsychiatric comorbidities. To examine how CA1-specific KCNQ2 deficiency modulates neural network activity during acquired epileptogenesis, we selectively knocked down KCNQ2 in mouse CA1 via adeno-associated virus (AAV)-short hairpin RNA (shRNA) and explored limbic network alterations. Calcium activity of glutamatergic neurons, gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) ergic neurons, somatostatin-positive (SST+) interneurons, and parvalbumin-positive (PV+) interneurons was recorded using cell type-specific GCaMP expression with simultaneous CA1 electroencephalography (EEG). Multi-site EEG recordings from CA1, cornu ammonis 3 (CA3), retrosplenial agranular cortex (RSA), infralimbic cortex (IL), cingulate cortex area 1 (CG1), primary motor cortex (M1), and basolateral amygdala (BLA) were analyzed for spectral power, functional connectivity (FC), and phase-amplitude coupling (PAC). We observed spontaneous activity, novel object recognition, and social behaviors of the model mice. CA1 KCNQ2 knockdown increased calcium activity in all neuronal populations during the latency, with greater activation of SST+ than PV+ interneurons. Excitatory-inhibitory imbalance correlated with seizure severity. EEG analyses revealed a biphasic pattern: reduced low-frequency power, phase synchrony, and FC during the latency, followed by widespread hypersynchronization of power spectral density, mutual information, and phase synchrony during severe seizures. In the non-epileptic state, PAC analysis revealed that knockdown group developed a biased network configuration characterized by enhanced PAC directed toward the BLA and weakened CA3-M1 and M1-related coupling. This pattern was consistent with their behavioral phenotypes, including reduced central exploration, fewer open-arm entries, impaired novel object exploration, and decreased social preference. During generalized seizures, PAC underwent extensive reorganization, with strengthened coupling between the BLA and multiple brain regions and reduced M1-directed coupling. Intraperitoneally administered retigabine (RTG), a pan-KCNQ channel opener, partially alleviated these behavioral deficits and attenuated the abnormally potentiated long-range network activity. CA1 KCNQ2 knockdown not only disrupts the local excitatory/inhibitory balance but also promotes epileptogenesis by reshaping limbic-cortical network coupling patterns.

papers.title: From Variability to Synchrony: Non-linear Development of Auditory Neural Responses During the First Year of Life.
papers.abstract: In humans, the first year of life is characterized by rapid developmental changes, including substantial brain maturation. As a result, neural responses to auditory stimuli undergo marked changes during this period. In this study, we followed 69 infants across their first year of life and recorded high-density electroencephalography (hdEEG) at 2 weeks, 6 months, and 12 months postpartum. Infants were presented with pure beep tones to examine the development of neural responses to auditory stimulation. We analyzed event-related potentials (ERPs), inter-trial phase coherence (ITPC), and event-related spectral perturbation (ERSP) responses to the beep tones and controlled for arousal state during stimulus presentation. We found that with increasing age, neural responses became more pronounced and showed reduced trial-to-trial variability. Phase synchronization increased from 2 weeks to later developmental stages in a broad low-frequency range (0.5 Hz to 13.6 Hz), indicating improved temporal alignment of brain responses over time. However, phase synchronization decreased from 6 to 12 months, suggesting a developmental transition towards more differentiated brain activity. Taken together, these findings demonstrate that auditory maturation during the first year of life follows a non-linear trajectory driven by dynamic changes in neural synchronization, reflecting the progressive refinement of functional neural circuits. Our results thus provide a critical benchmark for understanding the neural dynamics underlying sensory development during this period.

papers.title: Development and EEG Assessment of a Virtual Reality Replica of a Prior Real Multisensory Environment Intervention.
papers.abstract: Multisensory environments (MSEs) are valuable therapeutic spaces for relaxation and stress relief, yet high costs and physical infrastructure limit accessibility. Immersive virtual reality MSEs (V-MSEs) offer a low-cost and scalable alternative to real MSEs (R-MSEs), but evidence is scarce. The aim of this study is an exploratory characterization of the electroencephalography (EEG) response to a V-MSE replica of a previous R-MSE intervention, using the original R-MSE data as a qualitative reference. After developing a V-MSE mirroring the original environment, 31 healthy participants underwent an adapted version of the protocol, and spectral and nonlinear features were computed from EEG recordings pre- and post-intervention. Analyses were performed within each environment, and comparisons between them remained qualitative. The alpha/beta ratio, negatively correlated with stress, was the only feature significantly increased in both conditions. In the V-MSE, frontal theta and the theta/beta ratio also increased significantly, whereas relative gamma power and Lempel-Ziv complexity decreased. Only in R-MSE, parieto-occipital alpha power rose significantly, whereas frontal delta power decreased. No feature changed significantly in opposite directions between settings. Evidence remains insufficient to establish V-MSEs as an alternative to R-MSEs, but this first EEG characterization of a V-MSE is encouraging enough to justify broader studies.

papers.title: Neural Tracking of Continuous Speech Is Sensitive to Socially "Engaging" Prosodic Features of Conversational Anecdotes.
papers.abstract: While there is growing research on how the brain "entrains" to speech, it is unclear whether neural speech tracking is sensitive to interpersonally relevant changes in a speaker's tone of voice (prosody), such as when people try to sound "engaging" while telling conversational anecdotes. Here, we employed neural speech tracking to test whether listeners' speech encoding is enhanced by what a conversation is about and how speakers express themselves. Thirty-one participants listened to "gossip-like" anecdotes varying in topic (interesting vs. boring) and vocal delivery (engaging vs. neutral prosody) while recording their EEG. Participants estimated how long they would be willing to continue the interaction based on what they heard in each trial ("time bidding"). Neural speech tracking was quantified using Gaussian Copula Mutual Information between speech envelopes and EEG, and alpha power was analyzed as a complementary index of attentional engagement. Behaviorally, listeners preferred interesting (vs. boring) anecdotes and engaging (vs. neutral) sounding speakers; the effect of using an engaging prosody on time bids was stronger for interesting topics. At the neurophysiological level, engaging prosody enhanced neural speech tracking at frontal sites only when anecdotes were interesting, suggesting that neural encoding of social prosody depended on listeners' motivation to attend to the contents of speech. Alpha power displayed a distinct interaction over left-anterior sites, with opposite prosodic patterns for interesting and boring anecdotes; exploratory analyses suggested that lower left-anterior alpha power was associated with stronger neural speech tracking. Our study suggests that prosodic cues designed to engage a listener's attention enhance neural tracking of continuous speech, although these effects are constrained by broader contextual factors such as topic interest. These findings suggest that socially motivated vocal expression influences listeners' online neural encoding and highlight the importance of studying speech processing within its interpersonal communicative context.

papers.title: A Latent Variable Perspective on EEG Measures of Attentional Control
papers.abstract: Attentional control is a core cognitive function, yet there is still a significant debate revolving around its definition, factorial structure and underlying neural mechanisms. Research in this domain has largely developed along two largely disconnected traditions. Psychometric approaches assess individual differences using latent-variable models (e.g., structural equation modeling, confirmatory factor analysis), while cognitive neuroscience focuses on group-level behavioral and neural effects. This raises a critical question: can neural measures robust at the group level validly capture stable individual differences? Or more specifically, can some of the principles and analytical methods adopted in individual-differences research be directly applied to neural correlates of attentional control? The current study aims to address this question. Electroencephalogram data were recorded from participants as they completed four attentional control paradigms: a change detection task, the go/no-go task, the Simon task, and the Stroop task. From each task, we extracted the P3 component and a data-driven decoding accuracy measure as indices of conflict processing and tested whether these neural measures load onto a common latent factor of attentional control. Results revealed weak and largely non-significant correlations. Structural-equation modeling provided no evidence for a common latent factor, despite robust within-task effects at the group level reflected both in the behavioral and the EEG parameters. These findings suggest that EEG components may lack the construct validity needed to reliably capture individual differences in attentional control.

papers.title: Lesions of anterior cingulate cortex disrupt an electrophysiological signature of goal completion in humans.
papers.abstract: The reward positivity (RewP) is an event-related brain potential (ERP) component associated with feedback and goal completion. Although the component is said to be generated in anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), this inference is disputed because of the inverse problem. Recent intracranial electroencephalogram (EEG) current source density analyses provided direct evidence that the RewP is generated in caudal ACC, specifically Brodmann areas 24c' and 32'. To further test this hypothesis, we examined the effects of damage to frontal cortex damage on RewP amplitude. Scalp EEG was recorded from 68 stroke patients with frontal lesions while they performed a trial-and-error guessing task used to elicit a canonical RewP. Non-parametric voxel-based lesion-symptom mapping revealed that damage to Brodmann areas 24c' and 32' significantly attenuated RewP amplitude. These results align with evidence suggesting a single generator of the RewP in the caudal ACC, supporting the role of caudal ACC in motivation of extended behaviors.

papers.title: Adoption of Routine Intraoperative Raw EEG at a Quaternary Pediatric Centre.
papers.abstract: Intraoperative electroencephalography (EEG) allows real-time assessment of the anesthetic state of the brain and offers a means of titrating anesthetic delivery in children. Randomized trials have shown that EEG-guided titration reduces anesthetic exposure, shortens emergence and recovery, and lowers the incidence of emergence delirium, yet routine use outside research settings has remained largely confined to enthusiastic clinicians and clinical trials. To describe the adoption of routine intraoperative raw EEG monitoring over time at a quaternary pediatric hospital, to characterize practice variation among anesthesia providers, and to identify patient and procedural factors associated with EEG use. We conducted a retrospective single-center study of anesthetic records in the electronic health record from 17 October 2024, when automated EEG capture began, to 30 June 2026, following departmental implementation of routine raw EEG monitoring. Providers were categorized by EEG use as high (> 40% of cases), moderate (20%-40%) or low (< 20%). Trend, provider-level, and procedural associations with EEG use were examined using segmented regression, mixed-effects logistic regression, and clustered logistic regression. Of 26 168 analyzed cases, 21.7% (5674) involved intraoperative EEG monitoring, provided by 59 staff anesthesiologists, 9 senior fellows, 24 fellows, and 102 residents. EEG use rose from 17.8% of cases in October 2024 to 28.4% in June 2026. Use varied widely among staff anesthesiologists (median 18.1%, IQR 12.3%-31.3%; range 0.9%-79.5%); 59.3% (35/59) were low users, and 18.6% (11/59) were high users, with the five highest users accounting for 27.0% of all EEG-monitored cases managed by staff. Case mix explained only a small proportion of this variation (pseudo R2 = 0.064). EEG-monitored cases were more often longer, involved neuromuscular blockade, TIVA maintenance, cardiac surgery, and trainee presence. Adoption of routine raw EEG monitoring increased steadily but nonlinearly following implementation. Variation in use among providers was only weakly explained by case mix, indicating that individual practice patterns, more than patient or procedural characteristics, drove uptake. Efforts to broaden EEG monitoring may benefit from targeting low-use providers and during fellowship training.

papers.title: Toward Closed-Loop Cognitive Modulation in Alzheimer's Disease: BCI-Relevant Evidence and a Translational Roadmap.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) has entered a biomarker-defined era, yet most cognitive and neuromodulatory interventions continue to use fixed targets, timing, and doses. This targeted narrative review maps brain-computer interface (BCI) and closed-loop-relevant evidence in AD and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) by examining how sensing, control, and intervention modules are used prospectively. Read modules include electroencephalography (EEG), functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), real-time functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), functional ultrasound (fUS) and transcranial ultrasound localization microscopy (t-ULM), and digital measures. Control functions include feature extraction, within-person state decoding, uncertainty-aware decision rules, target-engagement assessment, and safety oversight. Write modules include neurofeedback, sensory gamma and sleep-phase acoustic stimulation, transcranial alternating-current stimulation (tACS), transcranial direct-current stimulation (tDCS), repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), transcranial pulse stimulation (TPS), transcranial ultrasound stimulation (TUS), transcranial photobiomodulation (tPBM), and focused ultrasound-mediated blood-brain barrier (FUS-BBB) opening. Human studies have separately demonstrated signal-contingent feedback, individualized targeting, physiological target engagement, home delivery, and emerging sensing, while preclinical studies provide mechanistic support for gamma, optical, and ultrasound approaches. Sleep-phase acoustic stimulation additionally demonstrates early automated signal-to-stimulus control. Passive sensing provides observations, personalization sets baseline parameters, state-informed control uses current signals to alter delivery, and target engagement verifies the proximal response without establishing clinical efficacy. Reliable decoding of waking cognitive states, broader controller utility, and durable clinical benefit remain unvalidated. We therefore organize the field around disease context, state sensing, feature extraction, state decoding, bounded decision/intervention, response verification, and safety oversight. The decisive early design compares assignments to an adaptive policy with otherwise matched fixed delivery; a sham arm can additionally test intervention efficacy. Such trials must prespecify decoder calibration, uncertainty, abstention, safety limits, and mechanistic and clinical endpoints. Closed-loop cognitive modulation therefore defines a translational research agenda for AD.

papers.title: Impaired cortical gap-mediated inhibition in chronic tinnitus but with limited individual diagnostic accuracy
papers.abstract: Tinnitus lacks an objective marker, limiting diagnosis and treatment evaluation. We tested whether gap-mediated inhibition of cortical sound-evoked responses provides one. In a prospective, multicentre case-control study at seven sites in the United States and Europe, adults with and without chronic tinnitus heard brief pulses preceded or not by a silent gap, embedded in broadband or narrowband carriers, during electroencephalography. The primary outcome was inhibition of the N100 response. Of 584 eligible participants, 455 yielded high-quality recordings with complete covariate data (232 cases, 223 controls; mean age 45.4 years, 52% women) that entered the adjusted analyses. Inhibition was strongest for broadband noise whereas narrowband carriers gave limited dynamic range. Participants with tinnitus showed reduced broadband gap-mediated inhibition ({beta} = -19.27%, d = -0.413, cluster-corrected p = 0.002), scaling with tinnitus severity (covariate-adjusted {surd}THI model: partial R2 = 0.049, p = 0.0015). In contrast, discrimination of individuals was limited (AUC 0.612, 95% CI 0.560-0.663). Cortical gap inhibition is a reproducible group-level effect rather than an individual diagnostic test.

papers.title: Differential associations of contralesional and ipsilesional brain functional connectivity with lower-limb impairment after stroke.
papers.abstract: Stroke may induce distinct plastic structural changes within the ipsilesional and contralesional hemispheres of the brain, leading to interhemispheric imbalances in cortical connectivity. Maximum joint range of motion (ROMmax) impairments may also occur in the paretic limb, contributing to increased interlimb asymmetry and impaired gait. This study examined the influence of ipsilesional and contralesional brain functional connectivity on hip flexion ROMmax interlimb asymmetry and walking performance in stroke survivors. Eighteen individuals with chronic stroke (57.5 ± 14.8 years; 26.7 ± 22.2 months post-stroke) were assessed for functional connectivity of the ipsilesional and contralesional general hemispheres and specific primary motor cortex (M1) areas of the brain with resting-state electroencephalography (EEG). Participants were also assessed for hip flexion active ROMmax of the paretic and non-paretic limbs and 10-m walk test, and ROMmax interlimb asymmetry was further calculated. Relationships between changes in these variables were examined by Pearson product-moment (r) and regression analyses. Hip flexion ROMmax interlimb asymmetry was significantly associated with contralesional functional connectivity in both general (r = 0.53) and M1-specific (r = 0.48) regions of the brain (P < 0.05). Walking performance was only associated with contralesional M1 connectivity (r = 0.51; P < 0.05). Contralesional hemisphere connectivity explained 28% of the variance in ROMmax asymmetry, while contralesional M1 connectivity explained 26% of the variance in walking time. No significant relationships were found for brain connectivity within the ipsilesional hemisphere. Greater brain functional connectivity in contralesional cortical regions is associated with increased hip ROMmax asymmetry and impaired walking performance in stroke survivors, highlighting the role of contralesional networks in post-stroke motor impairment.

papers.title: Microstate-specific functional connectivity in alcohol use disorder using resting-state EEG.
papers.abstract: Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD) is often described as a "disconnection syndrome", reflecting neural dysfunction associated with chronic alcohol use. However, previous studies on functional connectivity of resting-state EEG (rsEEG) in AUD have reported inconsistent findings, possibly due to overlooking the brain's dynamic nature. We examined rsEEG in 26 young adults with AUD and 35 healthy controls (HC), using microstate analysis to characterise transient brain states and to estimate functional connectivity within each state. Although microstate map topologies were comparable between the two groups, the temporal dynamics of the AUD group were biased towards microstates C and D. Particularly within microstate C, the AUD group showed significantly greater functional connectivity across most frontal-occipital channel pairs, whereas significantly reduced functional connectivity was observed in the interhemispheric channel pairs. Moreover, compared with conventional functional connectivity estimates, microstate-specific functional connectivity yielded superior classification performance in distinguishing the two groups. In addition, the AUD group showed less stable hub-like properties in microstate C, indicating diminished network efficiency. Our findings suggest that transient EEG properties, exemplified by microstate-specific functional connectivity, provide informative neural markers for characterising the impact of alcohol use on the brain.

papers.title: Invasive monitoring and mapping in epilepsy surgery: Acute and chronic intracranial recording from surface to depth.
papers.abstract: Invasive intracranial recording remains central to the surgical evaluation of drug-resistant focal epilepsy when noninvasive data are insufficient to define the epileptogenic zone or its relationship to eloquent cortex. This review, part of an International League Against Epilepsy (ILAE) Surgical Therapies Commission education series aligned with the epilepsy surgery curriculum, reviews invasive monitoring and mapping for the practicing and trainee epilepsy surgeon. Consistent with the competency-based ILAE epilepsy surgery curriculum, in which the surgeon is expected to understand and actively contribute to electrode selection, safe implantation, and the interpretation of invasive recordings within the multidisciplinary team, we give particular emphasis to the surgical execution of these methods alongside their electrophysiological rationale. We outline the historical development of the field from intraoperative electrocorticography and subdural recording to stereoelectroencephalography (SEEG), describe acute and chronic recording strategies using both surface and depth approaches, including the operative techniques of implantation and post-implantation electrode localization, and summarize the techniques of functional mapping. We compare subdural and stereotactic methods with respect to coverage, mapping capability, diagnostic yield, seizure outcome, and morbidity, and we review the complication profiles of each. Finally, we discuss future directions, including high-density and chronically implantable probes that combine macro-contacts with microelectrode recording throughout the electrode shaft. We emphasize that the choice of method should follow a clearly stated anatomo-electro-clinical hypothesis, balancing the completeness of sampling against procedural risk.

papers.title: Distinct cortical functional network alterations in internet gaming disorder and alcohol use disorder: A resting-state EEG graph theory analysis.
papers.abstract: Internet gaming disorder (IGD) and alcohol use disorder (AUD) are characterized by compulsive behaviors and impaired impulse control. Although IGD is classified as a behavioral addiction and AUD as a substance use disorder, previous studies have suggested potential neurophysiological similarities between the two conditions. However, the frequency-specific topological organization of cortical networks in IGD and AUD remains poorly understood. This study compared the cortical functional networks in IGD and AUD using resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) and graph theory-based network analysis. A total of 151 subjects (49 patients with IGD, 48 with AUD, and 54 healthy controls (HCs)) participated in this study. Resting-state EEG data were preprocessed, followed by source reconstruction and network analysis. We examined global and nodal network characteristics across different frequency bands. At the global network level, IGD exhibited a significantly higher clustering coefficient (CC) and strength (weighted degree) in the beta frequency band compared to AUD and HCs. At the nodal level, the IGD group displayed significantly increased beta-band CCs and strengths in multiple brain regions, particularly the parietal and limbic areas. Notably, beta-band nodal CC and strength in the bilateral superior frontal gyri were significantly lower in AUD than in IGD. Beta-band nodal CC and strength measures showed nominal associations with AUDIT or IAT scores. Our findings suggest that IGD and AUD exhibit distinct cortical network patterns. The results provide further neurophysiological evidence distinguishing IGD, as an example of behavioral addiction, from alcohol-related substance addiction.

papers.title: A novel theta-frequency tACS approach for major depressive disorder: Initial findings from an open-label pilot study.
papers.abstract: Theta oscillations are implicated in the pathophysiology of major depressive disorder (MDD) and represent a promising neuromodulation target. This study investigates individualized theta-frequency (ITF) transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) in adults with moderate-to-severe MDD, and reports on the initial evaluation of feasibility, tolerability, and clinical and neurophysiological outcomes. In this open-label pilot study, adults with MDD underwent a 20-session course of theta-frequency tACS (1.5 mA peak-to-peak; 20 min/session) applied bilaterally over the prefrontal cortex while performing working memory tasks. Theta stimulation frequency was individualized from pretreatment task-based electroencephalography (EEG) and recalibrated after 10 sessions. Montgomery-Asberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS) and EEG were assessed at baseline, midpoint (2weeks), and endpoint (4weeks), with MADRS repeated at 4-week follow-up. Ten of 11 enrolled participants completed all 20 treatment sessions and were included in analyses. Reported side effects were mild and transient. MADRS scores decreased significantly from baseline to midpoint, endpoint, and follow-up. At endpoint, response and remission rates were 80% and 60%, respectively; at follow-up, rates were 80% and 70% respectively. Greater increases in individualized theta frequency (ITF) power were associated with greater reductions in MADRS scores, although no significant group-level changes in ITF power were observed. The open-label design, absence of a sham comparator, and small sample size warrant cautious interpretation of these initial observations, particularly given the potential influence of placebo and expectancy effects. This pilot evaluation of individualized theta-frequency tACS in MDD demonstrates the feasibility of this novel approach and provides preliminary clinical and neurophysiological observations to inform future sham-controlled trials.

papers.title: Electrophysiological dynamics of empathy for self- and other-related pain
papers.abstract: Empathy requires the ability to generate shared representations of the self and others while maintaining a distinction between them. However, it remains unclear whether, and to what extent, the neural processes involved in sharing and understanding others' pain overlap with those involved in processing one's own pain, particularly with respect to their temporal dynamics. Therefore, the present study aimed to investigate the neural mechanisms underlying empathic processing of self- and other-related painful facial expressions. To this end, EEG signals were recorded from 42 female participants while they viewed self- and other-related painful and neutral expressions. During the early stage of processing, the difference in N2 amplitude between self-related and other-related stimuli was smaller in the painful than in the neutral condition. Nevertheless, self-related painful stimuli continued to elicit more negative N2 amplitudes and greater Alpha/Mu suppression than other-related painful stimuli. In contrast, during the late stage of empathic processing, no distinction was observed between self- and other-related painful stimuli. Instead, painful expressions, regardless of whether they were self- or other-related, elicited larger late positive potential (LPP) amplitudes. These findings suggest that empathic processing is characterized by an early self-other distinction followed by a later convergence in the neural representation of self- and other-related pain.

papers.title: Longitudinal exploration of auditory sensory-perceptual processing in CLN3 disease (Juvenile Neuronal Ceroid Lipofuscinosis (Batten disease)): A high-density auditory evoked potential (AEP) study.
papers.abstract: There is currently limited information about sensory and perceptual abilities across the progression of CLN3 disease (Juvenile Neuronal Ceroid Lipofuscinosis; Batten disease), a recessively inherited lysosomal storage disorder and a leading cause of childhood neurodegeneration. Clinical symptoms include vision loss, motor impairments, and cognitive challenges, making it difficult to accurately assess neurocognitive and perceptual abilities. Thus, there is a critical need to identify objective biomarkers that can be used to inform disease progression and track treatment response in this population. This exploratory case series investigates longitudinal changes in auditory sensory perceptual processing over several years in a small sample of individuals with genetically confirmed CLN3 disease (N = 4; 3 male) compared to a cross-sectional sample of 60 neurotypical (NT) controls using high-density electroencephalography (EEG). We utilized a duration mismatch negativity (MMN) paradigm, identical to what has been used in our previous cross-sectional study. We examined the auditory evoked potentials (AEPs) of the standard tones across three different stimulus onset asynchrony conditions and examined the N1 and P2 components of the AEP. Early evidence shows differences in the amplitudes of the N1 and P2 components in individuals with CLN3 disease relative to NT controls. These amplitude differences were most notable in CLN3 disease when participants were presented with standard tones that had the slowest presentation rate. Specifically, N1 and P2 amplitudes were more negative than NT controls in childhood and adolescence and as CLN3 disease participants aged, the amplitude of the AEPs was more positive than controls. Further, a more positive N1 amplitude during the longest stimulus presentation condition was associated with both reduced verbal intelligence and working memory abilities in CLN3 disease participants. Our preliminary case-series findings parallel recently published work in a mouse model of CLN3 disease that showed both sex- and age-dependent disruptions in central auditory processing. Taken together, we demonstrate the utility of auditory EEG measures as a sensitive, objective and translational measure in CLN3 disease that may serve as a potential outcome measure useful in tracking disease progression. Continued work is needed in humans focused on sex-based differences and longitudinal changes of auditory processing in CLN3 disease.

papers.title: Sensitivity of ECG QRS complexes to His-Purkinje structure in whole-heart electrophysiology models.
papers.abstract: A critical, yet understudied, determinant of patient-specific whole-heart electrophysiology (EP) model accuracy is the His-Purkinje system (HPS). The HPS influences ventricular depolarization and shapes the QRS complex of the electrocardiogram (ECG). In this study, we investigate how structural variations in the HPS models affect simulated QRS morphology for a complete whole-heart monodomain EP model, which includes all components of the cardiac conduction system. Using a rule-based fractal-tree algorithm, we generated HPS models and systematically varied nine structural parameters to evaluate their influence on ten QRS-related metrics. We used Sobol sensitivity analysis to quantify both direct effects and parameter interactions that drive observed variability in QRS metrics. Our results indicate that most minor perturbations in HPS structural parameters have limited impact on simulated QRS features. The variability induced by parameter perturbations across the 22,528 trials was neither substantially greater than the intrinsic stochastic variability of the network generation algorithm nor outside the bounds of normal QRS complexes. However, a small number of outlier trials deviated significantly. In particular, some generated HPS networks were overly dense and extended into the atrial region, leading to premature QRS complex formation, and a few others produced abnormal branching configurations that failed to adequately cover the ventricular circumference, resulting in abnormal QRS wave amplitudes and durations. These atypical HPS networks were extremely rare (<1% of the 22,528 models run) and could be readily identified and excluded from further use through quick visual inspection. Diagnostically relevant features of simulated QRS complexes in monodomain whole-heart electrophysiology models exhibited low sensitivity to moderate variations in HPS structural parameters in a healthy heart under sinus rhythm. Thus, a well-defined, generic HPS geometry is likely sufficient for most simulations of physiologically normal hearts in sinus rhythm, though some care should be taken to avoid abnormal, unphysiological networks revealed in this study. These findings represent a crucial step toward developing cardiac models that are robust to underlying anatomical uncertainties, ultimately enhancing their reliability for both research and clinical applications.

papers.title: Automated extraction of seizures and ictal-interictal continuum patterns from EEG reports to enable large-scale neurophysiology and neurocritical care research.
papers.abstract: Critical clinical information in EEG reports is often locked in free text, limiting large-scale research. This work develops and validates an automated, cross-institutional pipeline to extract seizures, rhythmic patterns, and ictal-interictal continuum features for population-level neurophysiology studies. We developed a five-stage hybrid pipeline comprising: (1) text normalization, (2) rule-based pattern filtering to focus the analysis on relevant report segments, (3) segment-focused prompt generation, (4) large language model (LLM) inference for structured attribute extraction, and (5) post-processing. This hybrid design combines the consistency of rule-based screening with the flexibility of LLM-based extraction from variable free-text EEG reports. The pipeline was applied to 156,582 EEG reports from three health systems (two adult, one pediatric). Performance was evaluated using a balanced set of 1,500 expert-reviewed samples, which extracted seizure presence, count, burden, and timing, as well as the frequency and prevalence of periodic and rhythmic patterns. Patterns included lateralized periodic discharges (LPD), generalized periodic discharges (GPD), and generalized/lateralized rhythmic delta activity (GRDA/LRDA). The pipeline achieved high performance across health systems for seizure (average accuracy 0.94) and periodic and rhythmic pattern detection (LPD: 0.97 [95 % CI: 0.94-0.99], GPD: 0.96 [0.92-0.98], GRDA/LRDA: 0.97 [0.94-0.99]). Seizure specificity was 0.72 at two adult institutions (95 % CI: 0.66-0.77) and 0.99 at the other two (one adult and one pediatric). Frequency and prevalence extraction showed strong agreement with mean values 0.94 and 0.93, respectively. High-frequency discharges (≥2 Hz) were associated with higher seizure occurrence within 24 and 48 h in descriptive analysis. This study introduces a scalable method for EEG analysis using clinical narratives, linking rhythmic patterns to seizure progression and supporting critical care risk stratification and large-scale EEG outcome prediction research.

papers.title: Report-derived interictal epileptiform discharge burden is associated with 7-day antiseizure medication decisions after pediatric video electroencephalography.
papers.abstract: To determine whether a three-level interictal epileptiform discharge (IED) burden abstracted from qualitative wording in issued pediatric video electroencephalography (VEEG) reports, rather than directly measured spike frequency, was associated with antiseizure medication (ASM) decisions within 7 days. This single-center retrospective cohort included 216 VEEG report episodes from 181 children. Two reviewers independently classified each report as showing no, low, or moderate-to-high IED burden while unaware of the standardized 7-day outcome; disagreements were adjudicated. We separately analyzed a diagnostic/initiation cohort for new ASM initiation and an established-epilepsy cohort for exploratory treatment intensification. Associations were assessed using exact and trend tests and logistic regression with patient-clustered robust standard errors. Agreement was 211/216 (97.7%); linear-weighted Cohen κ was 0.975 (patient-clustered bootstrap 95% CI 0.947-0.995). The diagnostic/initiation cohort comprised 113 reports from 112 children, with 36 new ASM initiations. Initiation rates were 13.0%, 42.9%, and 70.0% for no, low, and moderate-to-high burden, respectively (trend p < 0.001). The adjusted odds ratio per higher burden grade was 2.89 (95% CI 1.58-5.30; p < 0.001). The established-epilepsy cohort comprised 103 reports from 76 children, with 13 intensification events. Moderate-to-high burden versus none/low yielded an odds ratio of 4.73 (95% CI 1.31-17.08; p = 0.018), but complementary analyses were not statistically significant. Report-derived IED burden showed a strong graded association with new ASM initiation within 7 days. The treatment-intensification finding was exploratory. These data describe prescribing context and do not establish causality, treatment benefit, or an IED-based treatment threshold.

papers.title: Neurophysiological and Sleep-Related Effects of a Cosmetic Shampoo and Conditioner Regimen in Adults with Scalp Discomfort: A Pilot Study.
papers.abstract: Scalp discomfort is prevalent and associated with impaired quality of life and sleep disturbance. Although pruritus is linked to neurophysiological alterations and sleep disruption, these effects of cosmetic scalp care remain unexplored. This pilot study evaluated the neurophysiological and sleep-related effects of a cosmetic shampoo and conditioner regimen in adults with scalp discomfort and mild sleep disturbances. This observational pilot study enrolled 21 adults with scalp discomfort and sleep difficulties, of whom 20 were analyzed. After 1 baseline week and 1 washout week, participants used the cosmetic shampoo and conditioner at least three times weekly for 2 weeks. Neurophysiological outcomes were assessed with electroencephalography (EEG; arousal, valence, sleepiness, and anger levels) at baseline, post-washout, week 3, and week 4. Sleep was evaluated with the Stanford Sleepiness Scale, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, Epworth Sleepiness Scale, Insomnia Severity Index, and Fitbit Inspire 2 tracking. Scalp discomfort was assessed with a clinical report form. Data were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models. During the second reflective question set (Q2), EEG analysis showed significant improvements in mood valence (p < 0.001) and sleepiness (p = 0.021); arousal and anger levels did not change significantly. All four validated sleep questionnaires improved significantly: morning sleepiness decreased by 11.9% (p = 0.011) and overall sleep difficulty by 23.5% (p < 0.001) at week 3 and daytime sleepiness by 30.7% (p < 0.001) and insomnia severity by 35.9% (p < 0.001) at week 4. In an exploratory post hoc subgroup with below-average baseline deep sleep (n = 9), wearable tracking showed a 20.6% increase in deep sleep duration (p = 0.016); no significant change was observed in the full sample. Scalp itch intensity decreased by 49.1% (p < 0.001) and weekly discomfort days by 40.6% (p < 0.001). In this single-arm pilot study, use of the regimen was associated with improved scalp discomfort and with neurophysiological and sleep-related changes. Combining EEG, wearable tracking, and validated sleep instruments may offer a more objective framework for evaluating cosmetic scalp care. The deep sleep finding is hypothesis generating only. This study was retrospectively registered on 25 June 2026 on ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT07680608.

papers.title: Drug-resistant epilepsy: A retrospective observational study at a tertiary care hospital.
papers.abstract: To determine the prevalence and predictors of drug-resistant epilepsy among patients with epilepsy. A retrospective observational study was conducted at the Neurology Department of Liaquat National Hospital, Karachi, for the period from November, 2024 to October, 2025. Patients with epilepsy were enrolled, excluding neonates and those with psychiatric comorbidities or active substance abuse. Participants were recruited consecutively. Descriptive statistics summarized patient characteristics, while chi-square tests evaluated associations between variables such as drug adherence, epilepsy type, and antiepileptic drug (ASM) selection. Odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals were calculated to quantify the strength of these associations. A total of 382 participants were included (49.5% male, 50.5% female), with a mean age of 31.73 +/- 16.82 years and a mean seizure onset age of 25.3 years. The majority were urban residents with higher educational levels and 19.4% had refractory epilepsy. On multivariate logistic regression analysis, normal MRI brain findings (a OR = 0.29, 95% CI: 0.142-0.570; p < 0.001), normal EEG findings (a OR = 0.50, 95% CI: 0.256-0.974; p = 0.042) and adherence to the given treatment (a OR= 0.516, 95% CI: 0.234-1.138; p=0.101) have lower odds of having drug resistance. Lower level of education (a OR = 3.496, 95% CI: 1.687-7.245; p < 0.001), and a history of status epilepticus (a OR = 8.029, 95% CI: 4.186-15.400: p <0.001) have higher odds of refractory epilepsy. By identifying key predictors of drug-resistant epilepsy, our study contributes to a better understanding of factors associated with treatment resistance and may inform future interventions.

papers.title: Mismatched findings on ancillary examinations in virus-associated acute encephalopathy and encephalitis: pathological mechanisms and clinical significance.
papers.abstract: In this review, we group three mechanistically distinct categories of acute brain dysfunction after viral infection under the term "virus-associated acute encephalopathy and encephalitis": (1) viral encephalitis, caused by direct invasion and replication of neurotropic viruses in the central nervous system; (2) post-infectious autoimmune encephalitis, triggered by infection-induced central nervous system autoimmune responses; and (3) acute encephalopathy syndromes without direct central nervous system infection, resulting from systemic inflammatory storms or hypoxia. The three entities are grouped as a conceptual framework rather than an established classification because they all present as acute brain dysfunction occurring in association with viral infection and differ only in mechanism. The diagnosis of virus-associated acute encephalopathy and encephalitis relies mainly on ancillary examinations, including neuroimaging, cerebrospinal fluid analysis, and electroencephalography. In clinical practice, ancillary findings are frequently mismatched: some tests may be negative while others are positive, and results can evolve with the pathological mechanism and disease stage. Recognizing these mismatches can help clinicians identify the possible mechanism of central nervous system injury and avoid diagnostic and treatment delays, and guide further testing. In particular, empirical intravenous acyclovir should be started promptly when herpes simplex virus (HSV) or varicella-zoster virus (VZV) encephalitis is clinically suspected. This article reviews the mechanisms of virus-associated acute encephalopathy and encephalitis, and discusses the common causes of such mismatches and strategies to manage them; the proposed framework is hypothesis-generating and is not intended as a validated diagnostic algorithm.

papers.title: Neurophysiological changes following intensive Naikan therapy in a patient with recurrent depressive episodes later diagnosed with bipolar II disorder: A case report.
papers.abstract: Intensive Naikan therapy is a structured Japanese psychotherapy involving systematic reflection on interpersonal relationships; however, its neurophysiological correlates remain unclear. We herein report changes in resting-state electroencephalography (EEG), the P300 event-related potential, and standardized low-resolution brain electromagnetic tomography (sLORETA)-estimated source activity after intensive Naikan therapy. A 29-year-old man with recurrent depressive episodes and anxiety about family relationships and future employment underwent 7 days of inpatient intensive Naikan therapy. He was later diagnosed with bipolar II disorder after a hypomanic episode during the follow-up. Assessments were performed before and after the intervention. Anxiety decreased on State-Trait Anxiety Inventory state and trait scores (42 to 20 and 30 to 20, respectively), and depressive symptoms remained minimal on the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale and Beck Depression Inventory (4 to 3 and 0 to 0, respectively). Psychological measures suggested reduced self- and other-blame and greater acceptance of family members. Resting-state EEG showed a negligible change in peak alpha-band global field power, whereas peak beta-band global field power decreased from 5.13 × 103 to 2.84 × 103 µV2/Hz. During the auditory oddball task, P300 amplitude at Pz increased from 5.5 to 7.3 µV. sLORETA images were evaluated descriptively, without statistical comparisons or uncertainty estimations. Intensive Naikan therapy was temporally associated with reduced resting-state beta activity and an increased P300 amplitude. These observations from a single uncontrolled case with multiple assessments are hypothesis-generating and do not establish treatment efficacy, causality, or a treatment mechanism.

papers.title: Circadian rhythm in the atrioventricular node - in electrophysiology, contractility, metabolism, intracellular signalling and extracellular matrix
papers.abstract: The atrioventricular (AV) node shows a circadian rhythm-during sleep the PR interval is longer (because conduction velocity is decreased) and AV block is more common. We show the rhythm is similar in mouse and human, and using mice we have investigated the cause. There was still a rhythm in Kcnj5 knockout mice ruling out a major role of vagal tone (the vagus regulates the node via Kcnj5). Instead, we show the presence of a functioning circadian clock in the node (e.g. by detection of rhythmic clock transcripts). There was ~43-52% reduction in the rhythm of the PR interval on inhibition of the clock in a Bmal1 knockout mouse. There was a significant rhythm in >300 intracellular signalling molecules presumably driven by the clock and perhaps extrinsic signals. Downstream of the clock and signalling molecules, there was a rhythm in many transcripts and proteins (of 4,186 proteins, ~15% had a rhythm), responsible for example for contractile machinery, metabolism, extracellular matrix, and importantly ion channels. Ultimately, the PR interval is determined by ion channels, and there were rhythms in ion channels and ionic currents. A key determinant of conduction velocity is the upstroke velocity of the Ca2+-dependent nodal action potential and this was significantly reduced during sleep, this can be explained by reduced expression of Ca2+ channel subunits and a smaller L-type Ca2+ current at this time and this was confirmed by biophysically-detailed computer modelling. In conclusion, there is day-night molecular remodelling of the AV node and this is largely responsible for the circadian rhythm in the PR interval.

papers.title: A Novel DHX9 Variant Was Identified in a Patient With Developmental Delay, Facial Dysmorphism and Seizure.
papers.abstract: The DHX9 gene encodes an RNA helicase belonging to the DExD/H-box family, which is highly expressed in the brain and nervous system. Pathogenic variants in the DHX9 gene are associated with neurodevelopmental disorder (NDD) and Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (CMT). Both loss-of-function (LoF) and missense variants can cause NDD, whereas CMT is associated with specific missense variants. Patients with DHX9-related NDD typically present with intellectual disability, language and motor developmental delay, and autism spectrum disorder (ASD). CMT patients primarily present with distal weakness, sensory deficits, variable muscle wasting, foot deformities and painful sensory neuropathy. Here, we report a female patient with severe DHX9-related NDD phenotypes, including global developmental delay, ASD, facial dysmorphism, epilepsy, microcephaly, abnormal brain MRI findings and clinodactyly of the fifth finger. She experienced her first febrile seizure at 1 year and 2 months of age. She developed frequent myoclonic seizures characterized by rapid nodding and upper body tremors lasting 3-10 s at the age of 3 years. Simultaneous electroencephalogram (EEG) revealed paroxysmal bursts of high- to very-high-amplitude sharp-slow waves, spike-slow waves and polyspike-wave complexes diffusely over bilateral leads. Clinical exome sequencing (CES) identified a likely de novo missense variant in the DHX9 gene in the patient (NM_001357.5, c.1540C>T, p.(His514Tyr)). Notably, this variant resides within the highly conserved DEIH motif (Motif II) of the helicase ATP-binding domain. This critical region plays an essential role in ATP hydrolysis and helicase function. Three-dimensional protein structure modelling suggested that the p.(His514Tyr) substitution may compromise local protein stability by altering hydrogen bond networks. Our study expands the genetic and phenotypic spectrum of DHX9 variant-associated disorders.

papers.title: Coal Tar-Based Driveway Sealant Extract Induces Mutations in Liver, Bone Marrow, and Germ Cells of MutaMouse Male Mice.
papers.abstract: Coal tar-based driveway sealants (CTS) are a widespread but underrecognized source of human exposure to mutagenic polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs). We used Duplex Sequencing, an error-corrected sequencing technology, to assess the mutagenicity of a complex PAH mixture extracted from a CTS in MutaMouse male mice. We observed significant dose-dependent increases in mutation frequency (MF) in liver and bone marrow, with mutation spectra dominated by C:G > A:T substitutions, closely resembling a mutational signature linked to human cancers associated with tobacco smoking. In germ cells, we did not observe a statistically significant increase in MF, although there was a positive dose-response trend and enrichment of C:G > A:T mutations at higher doses. The mutagenic effects of CTS in germ cells were supported by a statistically significant increase in mutant frequency measured using the plaque-based lacZ assay. Tissue-specific analyses revealed greater mutation susceptibility and potency in liver, likely reflecting its central role in PAH metabolism. Mutation spectrum analysis showed that the mutagenic profile of the CTS extract largely resembled that of benzo(a)pyrene; however, detailed spectral analysis indicated additional contributions from other PAHs or PAH metabolites that produced distinct mutational patterns. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that the CTS extract induces tissue-specific mutagenic responses driven by characteristic C:G > A:T mutations, offering mechanistic insight into how environmental PAH mixtures contribute to mutation burden and cancer risk.
